<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1134653256">.mw-parser-output .side-box{margin:4px 0;box-sizing:border-box;border:1px solid #aaa;font-size:88%;line-height:1.25em;background-color:#f9f9f9;display:flow-root}.mw-parser-output .side-box-abovebelow,.mw-parser-output .side-box-text{padding:0.25em 0.9em}.mw-parser-output .side-box-image{padding:2px 0 2px 0.9em;text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .side-box-imageright{padding:2px 0.9em 2px 0;text-align:center}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output .side-box-flex{display:flex;align-items:center}.mw-parser-output .side-box-text{flex:1}}@media(min-width:720px){.mw-parser-output .side-box{width:238px}.mw-parser-output .side-box-right{clear:right;float:right;margin-left:1em}.mw-parser-output .side-box-left{margin-right:1em}}</style><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1092331828">@media(min-width:720px){.mw-parser-output .contains-special-characters{width:22em}}</style><div class="side-box metadata side-box-right contains-special-characters noprint selfref"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1126788409"/>

<div class="side-box-image"><img alt="Bengali" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Bengali_Conjunct_Kssya.svg/40px-Bengali_Conjunct_Kssya.svg.png" decoding="async" width="40" height="40" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Bengali_Conjunct_Kssya.svg/60px-Bengali_Conjunct_Kssya.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Bengali_Conjunct_Kssya.svg/80px-Bengali_Conjunct_Kssya.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="100" data-file-height="100" /></div>
<div class="side-box-text plainlist"><b>This article contains <a href="/wiki/Bengali_alphabet" title="Bengali alphabet">Bengali text</a>.</b> Without proper <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Bangla_script_display_help" title="Wikipedia:Bangla script display help">rendering support</a>, you may see <a href="/wiki/Specials_(Unicode_block)#Replacement_character" title="Specials (Unicode block)">question marks, boxes, or other symbols</a>.</div></div>
</div>
<p><b>Bangladesh</b> (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˌ/: secondary stress follows">ˌ</span><span title="&#39;b&#39; in &#39;buy&#39;">b</span><span title="/æ/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;bad&#39;">æ</span><span title="/ŋ/: &#39;ng&#39; in &#39;sing&#39;">ŋ</span><span title="/ɡ/: &#39;g&#39; in &#39;guy&#39;">ɡ</span><span title="&#39;l&#39; in &#39;lie&#39;">l</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;d&#39; in &#39;dye&#39;">d</span><span title="/ɛ/: &#39;e&#39; in &#39;dress&#39;">ɛ</span><span title="/ʃ/: &#39;sh&#39; in &#39;shy&#39;">ʃ</span></span>,<span class="wrap"> </span><span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˌ/: secondary stress follows">ˌ</span><span title="&#39;b&#39; in &#39;buy&#39;">b</span><span title="/ɑː/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;father&#39;">ɑː</span><span title="/ŋ/: &#39;ng&#39; in &#39;sing&#39;">ŋ</span></span>-/</a></span></span>;<sup id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Bengali_language" title="Bengali language">Bengali</a>: <span lang="bn">বাংলাদেশ</span>, <small>pronounced&#160;</small><span title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA" lang="bn-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Bengali" title="Help:IPA/Bengali">[ˈbaŋlaˌdeʃ]</a></span>&#32;<span class="nowrap" style="font-size:85%">(<span class="unicode haudio"><span class="fn"><span style="white-space:nowrap;margin-right:.25em;"><a href="/wiki/File:Bn-%E0%A6%AC%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%82%E0%A6%B2%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%A6%E0%A7%87%E0%A6%B6.oga" title="About this sound"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/11px-Loudspeaker.svg.png" decoding="async" width="11" height="11" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/17px-Loudspeaker.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/22px-Loudspeaker.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="20" data-file-height="20" /></a></span><a href="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0a/Bn-%E0%A6%AC%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%82%E0%A6%B2%E0%A6%BE%E0%A6%A6%E0%A7%87%E0%A6%B6.oga" class="internal" title="Bn-বাংলাদেশ.oga">listen</a></span></span>)</span>), officially the <b>People's Republic of Bangladesh</b>, is a country in <a href="/wiki/South_Asia" title="South Asia">South Asia</a>. It is the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population" title="List of countries and dependencies by population">eighth-most populous country</a> in the world, with a population exceeding 165 million people in an area of 148,460 square kilometres (57,320&#160;sq&#160;mi).<sup id="cite_ref-bdarea_7-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bdarea-7">&#91;7&#93;</a></sup> Bangladesh is among the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density" title="List of countries and dependencies by population density">most densely populated countries</a> in the world, and shares land borders with <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a> to the west, north, and east, and <a href="/wiki/Myanmar" title="Myanmar">Myanmar</a> to the southeast; to the south it has a coastline along the <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal" title="Bay of Bengal">Bay of Bengal</a>. It is narrowly separated from <a href="/wiki/Bhutan" title="Bhutan">Bhutan</a> and <a href="/wiki/Nepal" title="Nepal">Nepal</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Siliguri_Corridor" title="Siliguri Corridor">Siliguri Corridor</a>; and from <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a> by the Indian state of <a href="/wiki/Sikkim" title="Sikkim">Sikkim</a> in the north. <a href="/wiki/Dhaka" title="Dhaka">Dhaka</a>, the capital and <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bangladesh" title="List of cities and towns in Bangladesh">largest city</a>, is the nation's political, financial and cultural centre. <a href="/wiki/Chittagong" title="Chittagong">Chittagong</a>, the second-largest city, is the busiest port on the Bay of Bengal. The official language is <a href="/wiki/Bengali_language" title="Bengali language">Bengali</a>, one of the easternmost branches of the <a href="/wiki/Indo-European_languages" title="Indo-European languages">Indo-European language family</a>.
</p><p>Bangladesh forms the sovereign part of the historic and <a href="/wiki/Ethnolinguistics" title="Ethnolinguistics">ethnolinguistic</a> region of <a href="/wiki/Bengal" title="Bengal">Bengal</a>, which was divided during the <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_India" title="Partition of India">Partition of India</a> in 1947.<sup id="cite_ref-EyetsemitanGire2003_13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-EyetsemitanGire2003-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> The country has a <a href="/wiki/Bengali_Muslims" title="Bengali Muslims">Bengali Muslim</a> majority. Ancient Bengal was an important cultural centre in the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a> as the home of the states of <a href="/wiki/Vanga_Kingdom" title="Vanga Kingdom">Vanga</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pundravardhana" title="Pundravardhana">Pundra</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gangaridai" title="Gangaridai">Gangaridai</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gauda_Kingdom" title="Gauda Kingdom">Gauda</a>, <a href="/wiki/Samatata" title="Samatata">Samatata</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Harikela" title="Harikela">Harikela</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Mauryan_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Mauryan Empire">Mauryan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gupta_Empire" title="Gupta Empire">Gupta</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pala_Empire" title="Pala Empire">Pala</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sena_dynasty" title="Sena dynasty">Sena</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chandra_dynasty" title="Chandra dynasty">Chandra</a> and <a href="/wiki/Deva_dynasty" title="Deva dynasty">Deva</a> dynasties were the last pre-Islamic rulers of Bengal. The <a href="/wiki/Muslim_conquests_in_the_Indian_subcontinent" title="Muslim conquests in the Indian subcontinent">Muslim conquest of Bengal</a> began in 1204 when <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Bakhtiyar_Khalji" class="mw-redirect" title="Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji">Bakhtiar Khalji</a> overran northern Bengal and <a href="/wiki/Islamic_invasion_of_Tibet" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamic invasion of Tibet">invaded Tibet</a>. Becoming part of the <a href="/wiki/Delhi_Sultanate" title="Delhi Sultanate">Delhi Sultanate</a>, three city-states emerged in the 14th century with much of eastern Bengal being ruled from <a href="/wiki/Sonargaon" title="Sonargaon">Sonargaon</a>. <a href="/wiki/Sufi" class="mw-redirect" title="Sufi">Sufi</a> missionary leaders like <a href="/wiki/Sultan_Balkhi" title="Sultan Balkhi">Sultan Balkhi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Shah_Jalal" title="Shah Jalal">Shah Jalal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Shah_Makhdum_Rupos" title="Shah Makhdum Rupos">Shah Makhdum Rupos</a> helped in spreading Muslim rule. The region was unified into an independent, unitary <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Sultanate" title="Bengal Sultanate">Bengal Sultanate</a>. Under <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Empire" title="Mughal Empire">Mughal rule</a>, eastern Bengal continued to prosper as the melting pot of Muslims in the eastern subcontinent and attracted traders from around the world. The Bengali elite were among the richest people in the world due to strong trade networks like the <a href="/wiki/Muslin_trade_in_Bengal" title="Muslin trade in Bengal">muslin trade</a> which supplied textiles, such as 40% of Dutch imports from Asia.<sup id="cite_ref-Prakash_1450,_pp._237_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Prakash_1450,_pp._237-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Bengal" class="mw-redirect" title="Mughal Bengal">Mughal Bengal</a> became increasingly assertive and independent under the <a href="/wiki/Nawabs_of_Bengal" title="Nawabs of Bengal">Nawabs of Bengal</a> in the 18th century. In 1757, the betrayal of <a href="/wiki/Mir_Jafar" title="Mir Jafar">Mir Jafar</a> resulted in the defeat of Nawab <a href="/wiki/Siraj-ud-Daulah" class="mw-redirect" title="Siraj-ud-Daulah">Siraj-ud-Daulah</a> to the <a href="/wiki/British_East_India_Company" class="mw-redirect" title="British East India Company">British East India Company</a> and eventual British dominance across South Asia. The <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Presidency" title="Bengal Presidency">Bengal Presidency</a> grew into the largest administrative unit in <a href="/wiki/British_India" class="mw-redirect" title="British India">British India</a>. The creation of <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Bengal_and_Assam" title="Eastern Bengal and Assam">Eastern Bengal and Assam</a> in 1905 set a precedent for the emergence of Bangladesh. In 1940, the first <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Bengal" title="Prime Minister of Bengal">Prime Minister of Bengal</a> supported the <a href="/wiki/Lahore_Resolution" title="Lahore Resolution">Lahore Resolution</a> with the hope of creating a state in the eastern subcontinent. Prior to the <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_Bengal_(1947)" title="Partition of Bengal (1947)">partition of Bengal</a>, the Prime Minister of Bengal proposed a <a href="/wiki/United_Bengal" title="United Bengal">Bengali sovereign state</a>. A <a href="/wiki/Sylhet_referendum,_1947" class="mw-redirect" title="Sylhet referendum, 1947">referendum</a> and the announcement of the <a href="/wiki/Radcliffe_Line" title="Radcliffe Line">Radcliffe Line</a> established the present-day territorial boundary of Bangladesh.
</p><p>In 1947, <a href="/wiki/East_Bengal" title="East Bengal">East Bengal</a> became the most populous province in the <a href="/wiki/Dominion_of_Pakistan" title="Dominion of Pakistan">Dominion of Pakistan</a>. It was renamed as <a href="/wiki/East_Pakistan" title="East Pakistan">East Pakistan</a> with Dhaka becoming the country's legislative capital. The <a href="/wiki/Bengali_Language_Movement" class="mw-redirect" title="Bengali Language Movement">Bengali Language Movement</a> in 1952; the <a href="/wiki/East_Bengali_legislative_election,_1954" class="mw-redirect" title="East Bengali legislative election, 1954">East Bengali legislative election, 1954</a>; the <a href="/wiki/1958_Pakistani_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1958 Pakistani coup d&#39;état">1958 Pakistani coup d'état</a>; the <a href="/wiki/Six_point_movement" title="Six point movement">Six point movement</a> of 1966; and the <a href="/wiki/1970_Pakistani_general_election" title="1970 Pakistani general election">1970 Pakistani general election</a> resulted in the rise of <a href="/wiki/Bengali_nationalism" title="Bengali nationalism">Bengali nationalism</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pro-democracy" class="mw-redirect" title="Pro-democracy">pro-democracy</a> movements in East Pakistan. The refusal of the Pakistani military junta to transfer power to the <a href="/wiki/Awami_League" title="Awami League">Awami League</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Sheikh_Mujibur_Rahman" title="Sheikh Mujibur Rahman">Sheikh Mujibur Rahman</a> led to the <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War" title="Bangladesh Liberation War">Bangladesh Liberation War</a> in 1971, in which the <a href="/wiki/Mukti_Bahini" title="Mukti Bahini">Mukti Bahini</a> aided by India waged a successful <a href="/wiki/Revolution" title="Revolution">armed revolution</a>. The conflict saw the <a href="/wiki/1971_Bangladesh_genocide" class="mw-redirect" title="1971 Bangladesh genocide">1971 Bangladesh genocide</a> and the massacre of pro-independence Bengali civilians, including <a href="/wiki/1971_killing_of_Bengali_intellectuals" title="1971 killing of Bengali intellectuals">intellectuals</a>. The new state of Bangladesh became the first constitutionally <a href="/wiki/Secularism_in_Bangladesh" title="Secularism in Bangladesh">secular state</a> in South Asia in 1972.<sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islam</a> was declared the state religion in 1988.<sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup> In 2010, the <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh_Supreme_Court" class="mw-redirect" title="Bangladesh Supreme Court">Bangladesh Supreme Court</a> reaffirmed secular principles in the constitution.<sup id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>A <a href="/wiki/Middle_power" title="Middle power">middle power</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Indo-Pacific" title="Indo-Pacific">Indo-Pacific</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> Bangladesh is the second largest economy in South Asia. It maintains the third-largest <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh_Armed_Forces" title="Bangladesh Armed Forces">military</a> in the region and is a major contributor to <a href="/wiki/UN_peacekeeping" class="mw-redirect" title="UN peacekeeping">UN peacekeeping</a> operations. The large <a href="/wiki/Muslims" title="Muslims">Muslim</a> population of Bangladesh makes it the <a href="/wiki/Islam_by_country" title="Islam by country">third-largest Muslim-majority country</a>. Bangladesh is a <a href="/wiki/Unitary_state" title="Unitary state">unitary</a> <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_democracy" class="mw-redirect" title="Parliamentary democracy">parliamentary</a> <a href="/wiki/Constitutional_republic" class="mw-redirect" title="Constitutional republic">constitutional republic</a> based on the <a href="/wiki/Westminster_system" title="Westminster system">Westminster system</a>. <a href="/wiki/Bengalis" title="Bengalis">Bengalis</a> make up 99% of the total population of Bangladesh.<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> The country consists of <a href="/wiki/Divisions_of_Bangladesh" title="Divisions of Bangladesh">eight divisions</a>, <a href="/wiki/Districts_of_Bangladesh" title="Districts of Bangladesh">64 districts</a> and <a href="/wiki/Upazila" title="Upazila">495 subdistricts</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup> It hosts one of the largest <a href="/wiki/Rohingya_refugees_in_Bangladesh" title="Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh">refugee</a> populations in the world due to the <a href="/wiki/Rohingya_genocide" title="Rohingya genocide">Rohingya genocide</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup> Bangladesh faces many challenges, particularly <a href="/wiki/Corruption_in_Bangladesh" title="Corruption in Bangladesh">corruption</a> and <a href="/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change" title="Effects of climate change">effects of climate change</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> Bangladesh has been a leader within the <a href="/wiki/Climate_Vulnerable_Forum" title="Climate Vulnerable Forum">Climate Vulnerable Forum</a>. It hosts the headquarters of <a href="/wiki/BIMSTEC" class="mw-redirect" title="BIMSTEC">BIMSTEC</a>. It is a founding member of <a href="/wiki/SAARC" class="mw-redirect" title="SAARC">SAARC</a>, as well as a member of the <a href="/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation" title="Organisation of Islamic Cooperation">Organisation of Islamic Cooperation</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations" title="Commonwealth of Nations">Commonwealth of Nations</a>.
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Names_of_Bengal" title="Names of Bengal">Names of Bengal</a></div>
<p>The etymology of <i>Bangladesh</i> ("Bengali Country") can be traced to the early 20th century, when Bengali patriotic songs, such as <i>Namo Namo Namo Bangladesh Momo</i> by <a href="/wiki/Kazi_Nazrul_Islam" title="Kazi Nazrul Islam">Kazi Nazrul Islam</a> and <i>Aaji Bangladesher Hridoy</i> by <a href="/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore" title="Rabindranath Tagore">Rabindranath Tagore</a>, used the term.<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> The term <i>Bangladesh</i> was often written as two words, <i>Bangla Desh</i>, in the past. Starting in the 1950s, Bengali nationalists used the term in political rallies in <a href="/wiki/East_Pakistan" title="East Pakistan">East Pakistan</a>. The term <i>Bangla</i> is a major name for both the <a href="/wiki/Bengal" title="Bengal">Bengal</a> region and the <a href="/wiki/Bengali_language" title="Bengali language">Bengali language</a>. The origins of the term <i>Bangla</i> are unclear, with theories pointing to a <a href="/wiki/Bronze_Age" title="Bronze Age">Bronze Age</a> <a href="/wiki/Proto-Dravidian_language" title="Proto-Dravidian language">proto-Dravidian</a> tribe,<sup id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Austric" class="mw-redirect" title="Austric">Austric</a> word "Bonga" (Sun god), and the Iron Age <a href="/wiki/Vanga_Kingdom" title="Vanga Kingdom">Vanga Kingdom</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> The earliest known usage of the term is the <a href="/wiki/Nesari" title="Nesari">Nesari plate</a> in 805&#160;AD. The term <i>Vangaladesa</i> is found in 11th-century South Indian records.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-auto3_29-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto3-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> The term gained official status during the <a href="/wiki/Sultanate_of_Bengal" class="mw-redirect" title="Sultanate of Bengal">Sultanate of Bengal</a> in the 14th century.<sup id="cite_ref-Ahmed2004_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ahmed2004-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Shamsuddin_Ilyas_Shah" title="Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah">Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah</a> proclaimed himself as the first "<a href="/wiki/Shah" title="Shah">Shah</a> of Bangala" in 1342.<sup id="cite_ref-Ahmed2004_30-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ahmed2004-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> The word <i>Bangāl</i> became the most common name for the region during the Islamic period.<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> 16th-century historian <a href="/wiki/Abu%27l-Fazl_ibn_Mubarak" title="Abu&#39;l-Fazl ibn Mubarak">Abu'l-Fazl ibn Mubarak</a> mentions in his <i><a href="/wiki/Ain-i-Akbari" title="Ain-i-Akbari">Ain-i-Akbari</a></i> that the addition of the suffix <i>"al"</i> came from the fact that the ancient rajahs of the land raised mounds of earth 10 feet high and 20 in breadth in lowlands at the foot of the hills which were called "al".<sup id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> This is also mentioned in <a href="/wiki/Ghulam_Husain_Salim" title="Ghulam Husain Salim">Ghulam Husain Salim</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Riyaz-us-Salatin" title="Riyaz-us-Salatin">Riyaz-us-Salatin</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-riaj_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-riaj-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> The Indo-Aryan suffix <i>Desh</i> is derived from the Sanskrit word <i>deśha</i>, which means "land" or "country". Hence, the name <i>Bangladesh</i> means "Land of Bengal" or "Country of Bengal".<sup id="cite_ref-auto3_29-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto3-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="History">History</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Bengal" title="History of Bengal">History of Bengal</a> and <a href="/wiki/History_of_Bangladesh" title="History of Bangladesh">History of Bangladesh</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Ancient_Bengal">Ancient Bengal</span></h3>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Asia_800ad.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Asia_800ad.jpg/220px-Asia_800ad.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="127" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Asia_800ad.jpg/330px-Asia_800ad.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Asia_800ad.jpg/440px-Asia_800ad.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2099" data-file-height="1215" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Asia_800ad.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The earliest form of the <a href="/wiki/Bengali_language" title="Bengali language">Bengali language</a> developed during the <a href="/wiki/Pala_Empire" title="Pala Empire">Pala Empire</a>, shown here on a map of Asia in 800 CE.</div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara,_May_2017_47.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara%2C_May_2017_47.jpg/220px-Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara%2C_May_2017_47.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="125" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara%2C_May_2017_47.jpg/330px-Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara%2C_May_2017_47.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara%2C_May_2017_47.jpg/440px-Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara%2C_May_2017_47.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4160" data-file-height="2368" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Ruins_of_Somapura_Mahavihara,_May_2017_47.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Somapura_Mahavihara" title="Somapura Mahavihara">ruins of Paharpur</a> include a pyramid-like structure from the Pala period.</div></div></div>
<p><a href="/wiki/Stone_Age" title="Stone Age">Stone Age</a> tools found in Bangladesh indicate human habitation for over 20,000 years,<sup id="cite_ref-Bharadwaj2003_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bharadwaj2003-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources" title="Wikipedia:Citing sources"><span title="This citation requires a reference to the specific page or range of pages in which the material appears. (October 2021)">page&#160;needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> and remnants of <a href="/wiki/Copper_Age" class="mw-redirect" title="Copper Age">Copper Age</a> settlements date back 4,000 years.<sup id="cite_ref-Bharadwaj2003_35-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bharadwaj2003-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> Ancient Bengal was settled by <a href="/wiki/Austroasiatic" class="mw-redirect" title="Austroasiatic">Austroasiatics</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tibeto-Burman" class="mw-redirect" title="Tibeto-Burman">Tibeto-Burmans</a>, <a href="/wiki/Dravidian_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Dravidian people">Dravidians</a> and <a href="/wiki/Rigvedic_tribes" class="mw-redirect" title="Rigvedic tribes">Indo-Aryans</a> in consecutive waves of migration.<sup id="cite_ref-Bharadwaj2003_35-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bharadwaj2003-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-congress_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-congress-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> Archaeological evidence confirms that by the second millennium BCE, rice-cultivating communities inhabited the region. By the 11th century people lived in systemically aligned housing, buried their dead, and manufactured copper ornaments and black and red pottery.<sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Ganges" title="Ganges">Ganges</a>, <a href="/wiki/Brahmaputra" class="mw-redirect" title="Brahmaputra">Brahmaputra</a> and <a href="/wiki/Meghna" class="mw-redirect" title="Meghna">Meghna</a> rivers were natural arteries for communication and transportation,<sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> and estuaries on the Bay of Bengal permitted maritime trade. The early <a href="/wiki/Iron_Age" title="Iron Age">Iron Age</a> saw the development of metal weaponry, coinage, agriculture and <a href="/wiki/Irrigation" title="Irrigation">irrigation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> Major urban settlements formed during the late Iron Age, in the mid-<a href="/wiki/First_millennium_BCE" class="mw-redirect" title="First millennium BCE">first millennium BCE</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup> when the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Black_Polished_Ware" title="Northern Black Polished Ware">Northern Black Polished Ware</a> culture developed.<sup id="cite_ref-PierisRaven2010_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PierisRaven2010-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> In 1879, <a href="/wiki/Alexander_Cunningham" title="Alexander Cunningham">Alexander Cunningham</a> identified <a href="/wiki/Mahasthangarh" title="Mahasthangarh">Mahasthangarh</a> as the capital of the <a href="/wiki/Pundra_Kingdom" class="mw-redirect" title="Pundra Kingdom">Pundra Kingdom</a> mentioned in the <i><a href="/wiki/Rigveda" title="Rigveda">Rigveda</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> The oldest inscription in Bangladesh was found in Mahasthangarh and dates from the 3rd century BCE. It is written in the <a href="/wiki/Brahmi_script" title="Brahmi script">Brahmi script</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Greco-Roman_world" title="Greco-Roman world">Greek and Roman</a> records of the ancient <a href="/wiki/Gangaridai" title="Gangaridai">Gangaridai</a> Kingdom, which (according to legend) deterred the invasion of <a href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</a>, are linked to the fort city in <a href="/wiki/Wari-Bateshwar_ruins" title="Wari-Bateshwar ruins">Wari-Bateshwar</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-thedailystar1_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-thedailystar1-44">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> The site is also identified with the prosperous trading centre of Souanagoura listed on <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy%27s_world_map" title="Ptolemy&#39;s world map">Ptolemy's world map</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-google1_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google1-45">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> Roman geographers noted a large seaport in southeastern Bengal, corresponding to the present-day <a href="/wiki/Chittagong_District" title="Chittagong District">Chittagong</a> region.<sup id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Ancient <a href="/wiki/Buddhist" class="mw-redirect" title="Buddhist">Buddhist</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hindu" class="mw-redirect" title="Hindu">Hindu</a> states which ruled Bangladesh included the <a href="/wiki/Vanga_Kingdom" title="Vanga Kingdom">Vanga</a>, <a href="/wiki/Samatata" title="Samatata">Samatata</a> and Pundra kingdoms, the Mauryan and <a href="/wiki/Gupta_Empire" title="Gupta Empire">Gupta Empires</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Varman_dynasty" title="Varman dynasty">Varman dynasty</a>, <a href="/wiki/Shashanka" title="Shashanka">Shashanka</a>'s kingdom, the <a href="/wiki/Khadga_dynasty" title="Khadga dynasty">Khadga</a> and <a href="/wiki/Candra_dynasty" class="mw-redirect" title="Candra dynasty">Candra dynasties</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Pala_Empire" title="Pala Empire">Pala Empire</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Sena_dynasty" title="Sena dynasty">Sena dynasty</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Harikela" title="Harikela">Harikela</a> kingdom and the <a href="/wiki/Deva_dynasty" title="Deva dynasty">Deva dynasty</a>. These states had well-developed currencies, banking, shipping, architecture, and art, and the ancient universities of <a href="/wiki/Bikrampur" title="Bikrampur">Bikrampur</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mainamati" title="Mainamati">Mainamati</a> hosted scholars and students from other parts of Asia. <a href="/wiki/Xuanzang" title="Xuanzang">Xuanzang</a> of China was a noted scholar who resided at the <a href="/wiki/Somapura_Mahavihara" title="Somapura Mahavihara">Somapura Mahavihara</a> (the largest monastery in ancient India), and <a href="/wiki/Atisa" class="mw-redirect" title="Atisa">Atisa</a> travelled from Bengal to <a href="/wiki/Tibet" title="Tibet">Tibet</a> to preach Buddhism. The earliest form of the <a href="/wiki/Bengali_language" title="Bengali language">Bengali language</a> emerged during the eighth century. Seafarers in the <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal" title="Bay of Bengal">Bay of Bengal</a> where modern Bangladesh is now located, have also been sailing and trading with <a href="/wiki/Southeast_Asia" title="Southeast Asia">Southeast Asia</a><sup id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup> and exported Buddhist and Hindu cultures to the region since the early Christian era.<sup id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Islamic_Bengal">Islamic Bengal</span></h3>
<p>The early history of Islam in Bengal is divided into two phases. The first phase is the period of maritime trade with Arabia and Persia between the 8th and 12th centuries. The second phase covers centuries of Muslim dynastic rule after the Islamic conquest of Bengal. The writings of <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_al-Idrisi" title="Muhammad al-Idrisi">Al-Idrisi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ibn_Hawqal" title="Ibn Hawqal">Ibn Hawqal</a>, <a href="/wiki/Al-Masudi" title="Al-Masudi">Al-Masudi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ibn_Khordadbeh" title="Ibn Khordadbeh">Ibn Khordadbeh</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sulaiman_al-Tajir" title="Sulaiman al-Tajir">Sulaiman</a> record the maritime links between Arabia, Persia and Bengal.<sup id="cite_ref-auto5_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto5-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> Muslim trade with Bengal flourished after the fall of the <a href="/wiki/Sasanian_Empire" title="Sasanian Empire">Sasanian Empire</a> and the Arab takeover of Persian trade routes. Much of this trade occurred with southeastern Bengal in areas east of the <a href="/wiki/Meghna_River" title="Meghna River">Meghna River</a>. There is speculation regarding the presence of a Muslim community in Bangladesh as early as 690 CE; this is based on the discovery of one of South Asia's oldest mosques in northern Bangladesh.<sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-auto5_49-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto5-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> Bengal was possibly used as a transit route to <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a> by the earliest Muslims. <a href="/wiki/Abbasid" class="mw-redirect" title="Abbasid">Abbasid</a> coins have been discovered in the archaeological ruins of <a href="/wiki/Somapura_Mahavihara" title="Somapura Mahavihara">Paharpur</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mainamati" title="Mainamati">Mainamati</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> A collection of Sasanian, <a href="/wiki/Umayyad" class="mw-redirect" title="Umayyad">Umayyad</a> and Abbasid coins are preserved in the <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh_National_Museum" title="Bangladesh National Museum">Bangladesh National Museum</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Sultanate_period">Sultanate period</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Sultanate" title="Bengal Sultanate">Bengal Sultanate</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Delhi_Sultanate_Coin_from_Gaur,_Bengal_in_the_British_Museum.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Delhi_Sultanate_Coin_from_Gaur%2C_Bengal_in_the_British_Museum.jpg/250px-Delhi_Sultanate_Coin_from_Gaur%2C_Bengal_in_the_British_Museum.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="231" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/17/Delhi_Sultanate_Coin_from_Gaur%2C_Bengal_in_the_British_Museum.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="300" data-file-height="277" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Delhi_Sultanate_Coin_from_Gaur,_Bengal_in_the_British_Museum.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Coin featuring a horseman issued after the Muslim conquest of Bengal</div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png/220px-Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="230" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png/330px-Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png/440px-Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png 2x" data-file-width="1717" data-file-height="1792" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Map_of_Bengal_Sultanate.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Sultanate" title="Bengal Sultanate">Bengal Sultanate</a> and its vassals in the 15th-century.</div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg/220px-Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg/330px-Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg/440px-Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4200" data-file-height="2803" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Darashbari_Mosque_-012_Photo_by_Porag.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Mihrab" title="Mihrab">Mihrabs</a> and arches in the ruins of <a href="/wiki/Darasbari_Mosque" title="Darasbari Mosque">Darasbari Mosque</a>, an Islamic learning center of the Bengal Sultanate in the 15th century. Its roof collapsed during the <a href="/wiki/1897_Assam_earthquake" title="1897 Assam earthquake">1897 Assam earthquake</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg/220px-Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg/330px-Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg/440px-Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3648" data-file-height="2736" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Sixty_Dome_Mosque-01.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The 15th-century <a href="/wiki/Sixty_Dome_Mosque" title="Sixty Dome Mosque">Sixty Dome Mosque</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Mosque_City_of_Bagerhat" title="Mosque City of Bagerhat">Mosque City of Bagerhat</a> is the largest sultanate-era mosque in Bangladesh.</div></div></div>
<p>The Muslim conquest of Bengal began with the 1204 <a href="/wiki/Ghurid_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Ghurid Empire">Ghurid</a> expeditions led by <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Bakhtiyar_Khalji" class="mw-redirect" title="Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji">Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji</a>, who overran the Sena capital in <a href="/wiki/Gauda_(city)" class="mw-redirect" title="Gauda (city)">Gauda</a> and led the <a href="/wiki/Islamic_invasion_of_Tibet" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamic invasion of Tibet">first Muslim army into Tibet</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> Bengal was ruled by the Sultans of the <a href="/wiki/Delhi_Sultanate" title="Delhi Sultanate">Delhi Sultanate</a> for a century under the <a href="/wiki/Mamluk_dynasty_(Delhi)" title="Mamluk dynasty (Delhi)">Mamluk</a>, Balban, and <a href="/wiki/Tughluq_dynasty" class="mw-redirect" title="Tughluq dynasty">Tughluq dynasties</a>. In the 14th century, three city-states emerged in Bengal, including <a href="/wiki/Sonargaon" title="Sonargaon">Sonargaon</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Fakhruddin_Mubarak_Shah" title="Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah">Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah</a>, <a href="/wiki/Satgaon" class="mw-redirect" title="Satgaon">Satgaon</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Shamsuddin_Ilyas_Shah" title="Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah">Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah</a> and <a href="/wiki/Gau%E1%B8%8Da_(city)" title="Gauḍa (city)">Lakhnauti</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Alauddin_Ali_Shah" title="Alauddin Ali Shah">Alauddin Ali Shah</a>. These city-states were led by former governors who declared independence from Delhi. In 1352, Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah united the three city-states into a single, unitary and independent <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Sultanate" title="Bengal Sultanate">Bengal Sultanate</a>. The new Sultan of Bengal led the first Muslim army into <a href="/wiki/Nepal" title="Nepal">Nepal</a> and forced the Sultan of Delhi to <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Sultanate-Delhi_Sultanate_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Bengal Sultanate-Delhi Sultanate War">retreat</a> during an invasion. The army of Ilyas Shah reached as far as <a href="/wiki/Varanasi" title="Varanasi">Varanasi</a> in the northwest, <a href="/wiki/Kathmandu" title="Kathmandu">Kathmandu</a> in the north, <a href="/wiki/Kamarupa" title="Kamarupa">Kamarupa</a> in the east and <a href="/wiki/Orissa" class="mw-redirect" title="Orissa">Orissa</a> in the south. During the reign of <a href="/wiki/Sikandar_Shah" title="Sikandar Shah">Sikandar Shah</a>, Delhi recognised Bengal's independence. The Bengal Sultanate established a network of mint towns which acted as a provincial capitals where the <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_taka" title="History of the taka">Sultan's currency</a> was minted.<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> As Bengal became the easternmost frontier of the Islamic world, the Bengali language crystallized as an official court language during the Bengal Sultanate, giving rise to various prominent writers. The sultanate was evolving as a commercialized and monetized economy, and as a melting pot of Muslim political, mercantile and military elites.<sup id="cite_ref-auto1_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto1-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The two most prominent dynasties of the Bengal Sultanate were the <a href="/wiki/Ilyas_Shahi_dynasty" title="Ilyas Shahi dynasty">Ilyas Shahi</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hussain_Shahi_dynasty" title="Hussain Shahi dynasty">Hussain Shahi</a> dynasties. The reign of Sultan <a href="/wiki/Ghiyasuddin_Azam_Shah" title="Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah">Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah</a> saw the opening of diplomatic relations with <a href="/wiki/Ming_China" class="mw-redirect" title="Ming China">Ming China</a>. The reign of the Sultan <a href="/wiki/Jalaluddin_Muhammad_Shah" title="Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah">Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah</a> saw the development of <a href="/wiki/Bengali_architecture" class="mw-redirect" title="Bengali architecture">Bengali architecture</a>. During the early 15th century, Bengal aided the <a href="/wiki/Restoration_of_Min_Saw_Mon" title="Restoration of Min Saw Mon">Restoration of Min Saw Mon</a> in <a href="/wiki/Arakan" title="Arakan">Arakan</a>, which led to the latter becoming a tributary state of Bengal.<sup id="cite_ref-Chowdhury2004_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Chowdhury2004-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ChutintharanonChutintharānonBaker2002_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ChutintharanonChutintharānonBaker2002-58">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup> During the reign of Sultan <a href="/wiki/Alauddin_Hussain_Shah" class="mw-redirect" title="Alauddin Hussain Shah">Alauddin Hussain Shah</a>, Bengali forces penetrated deep into the <a href="/wiki/Brahmaputra_Valley" title="Brahmaputra Valley">Brahmaputra Valley</a>—and being led by <a href="/wiki/Shah_Ismail_Ghazi" title="Shah Ismail Ghazi">Shah Ismail Ghazi</a>, conquered <a href="/wiki/Kamata_Kingdom" title="Kamata Kingdom">Assam</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-r1_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-r1-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> Jajnagar in Orissa,<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Jaunpur_Sultanate" title="Jaunpur Sultanate">Jaunpur Sultanate</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pratapgarh_Kingdom" title="Pratapgarh Kingdom">Pratapgarh Kingdom</a> and the island of <a href="/wiki/Chandradwip" title="Chandradwip">Chandradwip</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Hasan2007p16-17_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hasan2007p16-17-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Hasan1987_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hasan1987-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> By 1500, Gaur became the fifth-most populous city in the world with a population of 200,000.<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> Maritime trade linked Bengal with <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a>, <a href="/wiki/Malacca_Sultanate" title="Malacca Sultanate">Malacca</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aceh_Sultanate" title="Aceh Sultanate">Sumatra</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bruneian_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Bruneian Empire">Brunei</a>, <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_India" title="Portuguese India">Portuguese India</a>, <a href="/wiki/East_Africa" title="East Africa">East Africa</a>, Arabia, Persia, Mesopotamia, <a href="/wiki/Yemen" title="Yemen">Yemen</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Maldives" title="Maldives">Maldives</a>. Bengali ships were among the biggest vessels plying the <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal" title="Bay of Bengal">Bay of Bengal</a>, <a href="/wiki/Indian_Ocean" title="Indian Ocean">Indian Ocean</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pacific_Ocean" title="Pacific Ocean">Pacific Ocean</a>. The Sultans permitted the opening of the <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_settlement_in_Chittagong" title="Portuguese settlement in Chittagong">Portuguese settlement in Chittagong</a>. The disintegration of the Bengal Sultanate began with the intervention of the <a href="/wiki/Suri_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Suri Empire">Suri Empire</a>. <a href="/wiki/Babur" title="Babur">Babur</a> began invading Bengal after creating the Mughal Empire. The Bengal Sultanate collapsed with the overthrow of the <a href="/wiki/Karrani_dynasty" title="Karrani dynasty">Karrani dynasty</a> during the reign of Akbar. However, the <a href="/wiki/Bhati_(region)" title="Bhati (region)">Bhati</a> region of eastern Bengal continued to be ruled by aristocrats of the former Bengal Sultanate led by <a href="/wiki/Isa_Khan" title="Isa Khan">Isa Khan</a>. They formed an independent federation called the <a href="/wiki/Baro-Bhuyan" title="Baro-Bhuyan">Twelve Bhuiyans</a>, with their capital in Sonargaon. The Bhuiyans ultimately succumbed to the Mughals after <a href="/wiki/Musa_Khan_of_Bengal" title="Musa Khan of Bengal">Musa Khan</a> was defeated.
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Mughal_period">Mughal period</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Subah" title="Bengal Subah">Bengal Subah</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:202px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Isa_Khan.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/42/Isa_Khan.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="308" class="thumbimage" data-file-width="200" data-file-height="308" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Isa_Khan.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Isa_Khan" title="Isa Khan">Isa Khan</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Zamindar" title="Zamindar">Zamindar</a> of <a href="/wiki/Sonargaon" title="Sonargaon">Sonargaon</a>, resisted Mughal expansion in the late 16th century</div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Bibi_Mariam.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Bibi_Mariam.jpg/220px-Bibi_Mariam.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="159" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Bibi_Mariam.jpg/330px-Bibi_Mariam.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Bibi_Mariam.jpg/440px-Bibi_Mariam.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="740" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Bibi_Mariam.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Bibi_Mariam_Cannon" title="Bibi Mariam Cannon">Bibi Mariam Cannon</a> (Lady Mary Cannon) was used by the <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Empire" title="Mughal Empire">Mughals</a> to defend their bases.</div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Lalbagh_fort.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Lalbagh_fort.jpg/220px-Lalbagh_fort.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="148" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Lalbagh_fort.jpg/330px-Lalbagh_fort.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Lalbagh_fort.jpg/440px-Lalbagh_fort.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3854" data-file-height="2597" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Lalbagh_fort.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The 17th-century <a href="/wiki/Lalbagh_Fort" title="Lalbagh Fort">Lalbagh Fort</a> was built by <a href="/wiki/Muhammad_Azam_Shah" title="Muhammad Azam Shah">Azam Shah</a>, who served as the <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Emperor" class="mw-redirect" title="Mughal Emperor">Mughal Emperor</a>.</div></div></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg/220px-Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="144" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg/330px-Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg/440px-Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5450" data-file-height="3559" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Asiatic_Society_Heritage_Museum.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Nimtali_arch" title="Nimtali arch">Nimtali arch</a> was the entrance to the palace of the <a href="/wiki/Naib_Nazim_of_Dhaka" title="Naib Nazim of Dhaka">Naib Nazim of Dhaka</a> who governed Dhaka, Chittagong and Comilla under the <a href="/wiki/Nawabs_of_Bengal" title="Nawabs of Bengal">Nawabs of Bengal</a>.</div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Mughal_Empire" title="Mughal Empire">Mughal Empire</a> controlled Bengal by the 17th century. During the reign of <a href="/wiki/Emperor_Akbar" class="mw-redirect" title="Emperor Akbar">Emperor Akbar</a>, the Bengali agrarian calendar was reformed to facilitate tax collection. The Mughals established Dhaka as a fort city and commercial metropolis, and it was the capital of <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Subah" title="Bengal Subah">Bengal Subah</a> for 75 years.<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> In 1666, the Mughals expelled the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Mrauk_U" title="Kingdom of Mrauk U">Arakanese</a> from Chittagong. Mughal Bengal attracted foreign traders for its <a href="/wiki/Muslin" title="Muslin">muslin</a> and silk goods, and the <a href="/wiki/Armenians_in_Bangladesh" title="Armenians in Bangladesh">Armenians</a> were a notable merchant community. A <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_settlement_in_Chittagong" title="Portuguese settlement in Chittagong">Portuguese settlement in Chittagong</a> flourished in the southeast, and a <a href="/wiki/Dutch_settlement_in_Rajshahi" title="Dutch settlement in Rajshahi">Dutch settlement in Rajshahi</a> existed in the north. Bengal accounted for 40% of overall <a href="/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company" title="Dutch East India Company">Dutch</a> imports from Asia; including more than 50% of textiles and around 80% of silks.<sup id="cite_ref-Prakash_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Prakash-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> The Bengal Subah, described as the <i>Paradise of the Nations</i>,<sup id="cite_ref-paradise_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-paradise-71">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup> was the empire's wealthiest province, and a major global exporter,<sup id="cite_ref-Prakash_70-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Prakash-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-richards95_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-richards95-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-riello_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-riello-73">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> a notable centre of worldwide industries such as <a href="/wiki/Muslin_trade_in_Bengal" title="Muslin trade in Bengal">muslin</a>, cotton textiles, silk,<sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Shipbuilding_in_Bangladesh" title="Shipbuilding in Bangladesh">shipbuilding</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ray174_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ray174-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> Its citizens also enjoyed one of the world's most superior <a href="/wiki/Standard_of_living" title="Standard of living">living standards</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-harrison_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-harrison-75">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-auto_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the 18th century, the <a href="/wiki/Nawabs_of_Bengal" title="Nawabs of Bengal">Nawabs of Bengal</a> became the region's <a href="/wiki/De_facto" title="De facto">de facto</a> rulers, with a realm encompassing much of <a href="/wiki/Eastern_South_Asia" title="Eastern South Asia">eastern South Asia</a>. The Nawabs forged alliances with European colonial companies, making the region relatively prosperous early in the century. Bengal accounted for 50% of the gross domestic product of the empire. The Bengali economy relied on <a href="/wiki/Textile_manufacturing" title="Textile manufacturing">textile manufacturing</a>, shipbuilding, <a href="/wiki/Saltpetre" class="mw-redirect" title="Saltpetre">saltpetre</a> production, craftsmanship, and agricultural produce. Bengal was a major hub for international trade, renowned for its silk and cotton textiles worldwide.<sup id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-77">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> Bengal was also famed as a shipbuilding hub.<sup id="cite_ref-auto_76-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-books.google.com_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-books.google.com-78">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Prakash_1450,_pp._237_14-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Prakash_1450,_pp._237-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Eastern Bengal was a thriving <a href="/wiki/Melting_pot" title="Melting pot">melting pot</a> with strong trade and cultural networks. It was a relatively prosperous part of the subcontinent and the center of the Muslim population in the eastern subcontinent.<sup id="cite_ref-star_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-star-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Bengali_Muslim" class="mw-redirect" title="Bengali Muslim">Bengali Muslim</a> population was a product of conversion and religious evolution,<sup id="cite_ref-google5_37-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-google5-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> and their pre-Islamic beliefs included elements of Buddhism and Hinduism. The construction of mosques, Islamic academies (madrasas) and Sufi monasteries (<a href="/wiki/Khanqah" title="Khanqah">khanqahs</a>) facilitated conversion, and <a href="/wiki/Islamic_cosmology" class="mw-redirect" title="Islamic cosmology">Islamic cosmology</a> played a significant role in developing Bengali Muslim society. Scholars have theorised that Bengalis were attracted to Islam by its egalitarian social order, which contrasted with the Hindu caste system.<sup id="cite_ref-Roy1999_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Roy1999-81">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> By the 15th century, Muslim poets were widely writing in the Bengali language. <a href="/wiki/Syncretic" class="mw-redirect" title="Syncretic">Syncretic</a> cults, such as the <a href="/wiki/Baul" title="Baul">Baul</a> movement, emerged on the fringes of Bengali Muslim society. The <a href="/wiki/Persianate" class="mw-redirect" title="Persianate">Persianate</a> culture was significant in Bengal, where cities like <a href="/wiki/Sonargaon" title="Sonargaon">Sonargaon</a> became the easternmost centres of Persian influence.<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1756, nawab <a href="/wiki/Siraj_ud-Daulah" title="Siraj ud-Daulah">Siraj ud-Daulah</a> sought to rein in the rising power of the <a href="/wiki/British_East_India_Company" class="mw-redirect" title="British East India Company">British East India Company</a> by revoking their free trade rights and demanding the dismantling of their fortification in Calcutta. A military conflict ensued which culminated in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey" title="Battle of Plassey">Battle of Plassey</a> on 22 June 1757.<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Robert_Clive" title="Robert Clive">Robert Clive</a> exploited rivalries within the nawab's family, bribing <a href="/wiki/Mir_Jafar" title="Mir Jafar">Mir Jafar</a>, the nawab's uncle and commander in chief, to ensure Siraj-ud-Daula's defeat.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Avari2013p137_86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Avari2013p137-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> Clive rewarded Mir Jafar by making him nawab in place of Siraj-ud-Daula, but henceforth the position was a figurehead appointed and controlled by the company.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> After Plassey, the Mughal emperor ruled Bengal in name only.<sup id="cite_ref-Lewis2011p48_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Lewis2011p48-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> Effective power rested with the company. Historians often describe the battle as "the beginning of British colonial rule in South Asia".<sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>The Company replaced Mir Jafar with his son-in-law, Mir Kasim, in 1760. Mir Kasim challenged British control by allying with Mughal emperor <a href="/wiki/Shah_Alam_II" title="Shah Alam II">Shah Alam II</a> and the Nawab of Awadh, Shuja ud-Daulah, but the company decisively defeated the three at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Buxar" title="Battle of Buxar">Battle of Buxar</a> on 23 October 1764.<sup id="cite_ref-Avari2013p137_86-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Avari2013p137-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Lewis2011p48_88-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Lewis2011p48-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> The resulting treaty made the Mughal emperor a puppet of the British and gave the company the right to collect taxes (<i><a href="/wiki/Dewan" title="Dewan">diwani</a></i>) in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, giving them de facto control of the region.<sup id="cite_ref-Lewis2011p48_88-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Lewis2011p48-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-vanSchendel2009p56_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vanSchendel2009p56-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup> The Company used Bengal's tax revenue to conquer the rest of India.<sup id="cite_ref-vanSchendel2009p56_90-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vanSchendel2009p56-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Colonial_period">Colonial period</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Presidency" title="Bengal Presidency">Bengal Presidency</a> and <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Bengal_and_Assam" title="Eastern Bengal and Assam">Eastern Bengal and Assam</a></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg/220px-Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="399" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg/330px-Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg/440px-Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2275" data-file-height="4123" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Jesuits_at_Akbar%27s_court.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Portuguese envoys (top left) at the imperial court of emperor <a href="/wiki/Akbar" title="Akbar">Akbar</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_settlement_in_Chittagong" title="Portuguese settlement in Chittagong">Portuguese settlement in Chittagong</a> flourished until the Mughals expelled the Portuguese in 1666.</div></div></div>
<p>Two decades after <a href="/wiki/Vasco_Da_Gama" class="mw-redirect" title="Vasco Da Gama">Vasco Da Gama</a>'s landing in <a href="/wiki/Calicut" class="mw-redirect" title="Calicut">Calicut</a>, the Bengal Sultanate permitted the <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Empire" title="Portuguese Empire">Portuguese</a> settlement in Chittagong to be established in 1528. It became the first European colonial enclave in Bengal. The Bengal Sultanate lost control of Chittagong in 1531 after Arakan declared independence and the established Kingdom of Mrauk U.
</p><p>Portuguese ships from Goa and <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Malacca" title="Portuguese Malacca">Malacca</a> began frequenting the port city in the 16th century. The <i><a href="/wiki/Cartaz" title="Cartaz">cartaz</a></i> system was introduced and required all ships in the area to purchase naval trading licenses from the Portuguese settlement. <a href="/wiki/Slave_trade" class="mw-redirect" title="Slave trade">Slave trade</a> and piracy flourished. The nearby island of <a href="/wiki/Sandwip" title="Sandwip">Sandwip</a> was conquered in 1602. In 1615, the <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Navy" title="Portuguese Navy">Portuguese Navy</a> defeated a joint <a href="/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company" title="Dutch East India Company">Dutch East India Company</a> and Arakanese fleet near the coast of Chittagong.
</p><p>The Bengal Sultan after 1534 allowed the Portuguese to create several settlements at Chitagoong, Satgaon,<sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> Hughli, Bandel, and Dhaka. In 1535, the Portuguese allied with the Bengal sultan and held the Teliagarhi pass 280 kilometres (170&#160;mi) from <a href="/wiki/Patna" title="Patna">Patna</a> helping to avoid the invasion by the Mughals. By then several of the products came from Patna and the Portuguese send in traders, establishing a factory there since 1580.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By the time the Portuguese assured military help against Sher Shah, the Mughals already had started to conquer the Sultanate of Ghiyasuddin Mahmud.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The region has been described as the "Paradise of Nations",<sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> and its inhabitants's <a href="/wiki/Standards_of_living" class="mw-redirect" title="Standards of living">living standards</a> and <a href="/wiki/Real_wages" title="Real wages">real wages</a> were among the highest in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> It alone accounted for 40% of <a href="/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company" title="Dutch East India Company">Dutch imports</a> outside the <a href="/wiki/Europe" title="Europe">European</a> continent.<sup id="cite_ref-Prakash_70-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Prakash-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-star_79-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-star-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> The eastern part of Bengal was globally prominent in industries such as <a href="/wiki/Textile_manufacturing" title="Textile manufacturing">textile manufacturing</a> and <a href="/wiki/Shipbuilding" title="Shipbuilding">shipbuilding</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-ray_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ray-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> and it was a major exporter of <a href="/wiki/Silk" title="Silk">silk</a> and <a href="/wiki/Cotton" title="Cotton">cotton</a> <a href="/wiki/Textile" title="Textile">textiles</a>, <a href="/wiki/Steel" title="Steel">steel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Saltpeter" class="mw-redirect" title="Saltpeter">saltpeter</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Agricultural" class="mw-redirect" title="Agricultural">agricultural</a> and industrial produce in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-star_79-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-star-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup>
In 1666, the Mughal government of Bengal led by viceroy <a href="/wiki/Shaista_Khan" title="Shaista Khan">Shaista Khan</a> moved to retake Chittagong from Portuguese and Arakanese control. The <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Mughal_War" title="Anglo-Mughal War">Anglo-Mughal War</a> was witnessed in 1686.<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Clive.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Clive.jpg/300px-Clive.jpg" decoding="async" width="300" height="234" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Clive.jpg/450px-Clive.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Clive.jpg/600px-Clive.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2400" data-file-height="1870" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Clive.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Lord_Clive" class="mw-redirect" title="Lord Clive">Lord Clive</a> meeting with <a href="/wiki/Mir_Jafar" title="Mir Jafar">Mir Jafar</a> after the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey" title="Battle of Plassey">Battle of Plassey</a>, which led to the overthrow of the last independent <a href="/wiki/Nawab_of_Bengal" class="mw-redirect" title="Nawab of Bengal">Nawab of Bengal</a></div></div></div>
<p>After the 1757 <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey" title="Battle of Plassey">Battle of Plassey</a>, Bengal was the first region of the Indian subcontinent conquered by the <a href="/wiki/British_East_India_Company" class="mw-redirect" title="British East India Company">British East India Company</a>. The company formed the <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Presidency" title="Bengal Presidency">Presidency of Fort William</a>, which administered the region until 1858. A notable aspect of <a href="/wiki/Company_rule_in_India" title="Company rule in India">Company rule</a> was the <a href="/wiki/Permanent_Settlement" title="Permanent Settlement">Permanent Settlement</a>, which established the feudal <a href="/wiki/Zamindar" title="Zamindar">zamindari</a> system; in addition, Company policies led to the <a href="/wiki/Deindustrialisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Deindustrialisation">deindustrialisation</a> of Bengal's textile industry.<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup> The capital amassed by the East India Company in Bengal was invested in the emerging <a href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</a> in <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland" title="United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland">Great Britain</a>, in industries such as <a href="/wiki/Textile_manufacture_during_the_Industrial_Revolution" class="mw-redirect" title="Textile manufacture during the Industrial Revolution">textile manufacturing</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-sengupta_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sengupta-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> Economic mismanagement, alongside drought and a smallpox epidemic, directly led to the <a href="/wiki/Great_Bengal_famine_of_1770" title="Great Bengal famine of 1770">Great Bengal famine of 1770</a>, which is estimated to have caused the deaths of between 1 million and 10 million people.<sup id="cite_ref-Roy2019_102-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Roy2019-102">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Jonsson2013p167_105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Jonsson2013p167-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> Several rebellions broke out during the early 19th century (including one led by <a href="/wiki/Titumir" title="Titumir">Titumir</a>), as Company rule had displaced the Muslim ruling class from power. A conservative Islamic cleric, <a href="/wiki/Haji_Shariatullah" title="Haji Shariatullah">Haji Shariatullah</a>, sought to overthrow the British by propagating Islamic revivalism.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> Several towns in Bangladesh participated in the <a href="/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857" title="Indian Rebellion of 1857">Indian Rebellion of 1857</a><sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> and pledged allegiance to the last Mughal emperor, <a href="/wiki/Bahadur_Shah_Zafar" title="Bahadur Shah Zafar">Bahadur Shah Zafar</a>, who was later exiled to neighbouring Burma.
</p><p>The challenge posed to company rule by the failed Indian Mutiny led to the creation of the <a href="/wiki/British_Indian_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="British Indian Empire">British Indian Empire</a> as a <a href="/wiki/Crown_colony" title="Crown colony">crown colony</a>. The British established several schools, colleges, and a university in Bangladesh. <a href="/wiki/Syed_Ahmed_Khan" class="mw-redirect" title="Syed Ahmed Khan">Syed Ahmed Khan</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ram_Mohan_Roy" title="Ram Mohan Roy">Ram Mohan Roy</a> promoted modern and <a href="/wiki/Liberal_education" title="Liberal education">liberal education</a> in the subcontinent, inspiring the <a href="/wiki/Aligarh_movement" class="mw-redirect" title="Aligarh movement">Aligarh movement</a><sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Renaissance" class="mw-redirect" title="Bengal Renaissance">Bengal Renaissance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> During the late 19th century, novelists, social reformers and feminists emerged from Muslim Bengali society. <a href="/wiki/Electricity" title="Electricity">Electricity</a> and municipal water systems were introduced in the 1890s; <a href="/wiki/Movie_theatre" class="mw-redirect" title="Movie theatre">cinemas</a> opened in many towns during the early 20th century. East Bengal's <a href="/wiki/Plantation_economy" title="Plantation economy">plantation economy</a> was important to the British Empire, particularly its <a href="/wiki/Jute" title="Jute">jute</a> and <a href="/wiki/Tea_production_in_Bangladesh" title="Tea production in Bangladesh">tea</a>. The British established <a href="/wiki/Free_port" class="mw-redirect" title="Free port">tax-free river ports</a>, such as the <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Narayanganj" title="Port of Narayanganj">Port of Narayanganj</a>, and large seaports like the <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Chittagong" title="Port of Chittagong">Port of Chittagong</a>.
</p><p>Bengal had the highest gross domestic product in British India.<sup id="cite_ref-daily-sun.com_110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-daily-sun.com-110">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> Bengal was one of the first regions in Asia to have a railway. The first railway in what is now Bangladesh began operating in 1862.<sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> In comparison, <a href="/wiki/Japan" title="Japan">Japan</a> saw its first railway in 1872. The main railway companies in the region were the <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Bengal_Railway" title="Eastern Bengal Railway">Eastern Bengal Railway</a> and <a href="/wiki/Assam_Bengal_Railway" title="Assam Bengal Railway">Assam Bengal Railway</a>. Railways competed with waterborne transport to become one of the main mediums of transport.<sup id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-112">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Supported by the Muslim aristocracy, the British government created the province of <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Bengal_and_Assam" title="Eastern Bengal and Assam">Eastern Bengal and Assam</a> in 1905; the new province received increased investment in education, transport, and industry.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> However, the <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_Bengal_(1905)" title="Partition of Bengal (1905)">first partition of Bengal</a> created an uproar in <a href="/wiki/Kolkata" title="Kolkata">Calcutta</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Indian_National_Congress" title="Indian National Congress">Indian National Congress</a>. In response to growing Hindu nationalism, the <a href="/wiki/All_India_Muslim_League" class="mw-redirect" title="All India Muslim League">All India Muslim League</a> was formed in Dhaka during the 1906 All India Muhammadan Educational Conference. The British government reorganised the provinces in 1912, reuniting East and West Bengal and making <a href="/wiki/Assam_Province" title="Assam Province">Assam</a> a second province.
</p><p>The Raj was slow to allow self-rule in the colonial subcontinent. It established the <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Legislative_Council" title="Bengal Legislative Council">Bengal Legislative Council</a> in 1862, and the council's native Bengali representation increased during the early 20th century. The <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Provincial_Muslim_League" title="Bengal Provincial Muslim League">Bengal Provincial Muslim League</a> was formed in 1913 to advocate <a href="/wiki/Civil_rights" class="mw-redirect" title="Civil rights">civil rights</a> for Bengali Muslims within a constitutional framework. During the 1920s, the league was divided into factions supporting the <a href="/wiki/Khilafat_movement" class="mw-redirect" title="Khilafat movement">Khilafat movement</a> and favouring co-operation with the British to achieve self-rule. Segments of the Bengali elite supported <a href="/wiki/Mustafa_Kemal_Atat%C3%BCrk" title="Mustafa Kemal Atatürk">Mustafa Kemal Atatürk</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Secularism_in_Turkey" title="Secularism in Turkey">secularist</a> forces.<sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> In 1929, the <a href="/wiki/Praja_Party" class="mw-redirect" title="Praja Party">All Bengal Tenants Association</a> was formed in the Bengal Legislative Council to counter the influence of the Hindu landed gentry, and the <a href="/wiki/Indian_Independence_Movement" class="mw-redirect" title="Indian Independence Movement">Indian Independence</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pakistan_Movement" title="Pakistan Movement">Pakistan Movements</a> strengthened during the early 20th century. After the <a href="/wiki/Morley-Minto_Reforms" class="mw-redirect" title="Morley-Minto Reforms">Morley-Minto Reforms</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Government_of_India_Act_1919" title="Government of India Act 1919">diarchy</a> era in the <a href="/wiki/Legislatures_of_British_India" title="Legislatures of British India">legislatures of British India</a>, the British government promised <a href="/wiki/Government_of_India_Act_1935" title="Government of India Act 1935">limited provincial autonomy</a> in 1935. The <a href="/wiki/Bengal_Legislative_Assembly" title="Bengal Legislative Assembly">Bengal Legislative Assembly</a>, British India's largest legislature, was established in 1937.
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:342px;"><a href="/wiki/File:All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg/340px-All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg" decoding="async" width="340" height="109" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg/510px-All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg/680px-All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="257" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:All_India_Muslim_league_conference_1906_attendees_in_Dhaka.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Founding conference of the <a href="/wiki/All_India_Muslim_League" class="mw-redirect" title="All India Muslim League">All India Muslim League</a> in Dhaka, 1906</div></div></div>
<p>Although it won most seats in 1937, the Bengal Congress boycotted the legislature. <a href="/wiki/A._K._Fazlul_Huq" title="A. K. Fazlul Huq">A. K. Fazlul Huq</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Krishak_Sramik_Party" title="Krishak Sramik Party">Krishak Praja Party</a> was elected as the first <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Bengal" title="Prime Minister of Bengal">Prime Minister of Bengal</a>. In 1940 Huq supported the <a href="/wiki/Lahore_Resolution" title="Lahore Resolution">Lahore Resolution</a>, which envisaged independent states in the subcontinent's northwestern and eastern Muslim-majority regions. The first Huq ministry, a coalition with the Bengal Provincial Muslim League, lasted until 1941; it was followed by a Huq coalition with the <a href="/wiki/Hindu_Mahasabha" title="Hindu Mahasabha">Hindu Mahasabha</a> which lasted until 1943.
